L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: We show that the number of (0, 1)-matrices with n rows and k columns uniquely reconstructable from their row and column sums is the poly-Bernoulli number B(−k) n . Combinatorial proofs for both the sieve and closed formulas are presented. In addition, we prove an
L9@P0: analogue of Fermat’s Little Theorem: For a positive integer n and prime number p we have
L10@P0: B(−p) n ≡ 2n (mod p). Also, an analogue to Fermat’s Last Theorem is presented: For all positive integers {x, y, z} and n > 1 there exist no solution to the equation B(−n) x +B(−n)
L11@P0: y = B(−n) z .

L13@P0: Our work concerns the set of binary matrices that can be described uniquely by their row

L198@P4: Lemma 1 (Symbol Weight). No two distinct symbols of the same weight occur in an
L199@P4: allowable word of our language.
L200@P4: Proof. If two distinct symbols occur in a given word, then exchanging these columns with
L201@P4: each other would not change the row or column sums, which would violate the Lonesum
L202@P4: definition.
L203@P4: By a similar argument, we have the following:
L204@P4: Corollary 1 (Row Weight). No two distinct rows can have the same weight in an allowable
L205@P4: word.
L206@P4: Lemma 2 (Swap). Permuting rows or columns does not change membership in the class
L207@P4: of Lonesum matrices.
L208@P4: Proof. Note that the forbidden minors are mirror images. Swapping either the rows or
L209@P4: columns of one forbidden minor will give you the other. Thus, any permutation of rows or
L210@P4: columns will still yield the same number of forbidden minors.

L362@P6: 3.3. An Analogue of Fermat’s Little Theorem
L363@P6: We can derive a poly-Bernoulli cohort to Fermat’s Little Theorem, which states that for any
L364@P6: positive integer a and prime number p,
L365@P6: ap ≡ a (mod p).
L366@P6: We will start with the main lemma of [1].
L367@P6: Lemma 5 (ABR 2005). Let S be a finite set, let p be a prime number, let f(x) : S → S be
L368@P6: a function that has the property f p(x) = x for any x in S, and let F be the number of fixed
L369@P6: points. Then
L370@P6: |S| ≡ |F| (mod p).
L371@P6: One could view the function f as a directed graph on elements in S consisting of disjoint
L372@P6: length p cycles and loops.
L373@P6: Theorem 4 (Row Ordered Fermat’s Little Theorem). Given a prime number p, and
L374@P6: a positive integer n,
L375@P6: B(−p) n ≡ 2n (mod p). (3)
L376@P6: Proof. Let S be the set of n × p Lonesum (0,1)-matrices. Let f be the function that rotates
L377@P6: the columns of a matrix once to the left. The matrices that are fixed points in this function
L378@P6: are those consisting of all one and all zero rows. There are 2n such matrices, so let F = 2n.
L379@P6: From the above lemma |S| ≡ |F| (mod p). Substituting for S and F we get B(−p) n ≡ 2n

L381@P7: 3.4. An Analogue of Fermat’s Last Theorem
L382@P7: Ernst Kummer in the 1800’s attempted to attack Fermat’s Last Theorem with the Bernoulli
L383@P7: numbers. His approach showed that for a prime number p, if p does not divide B(1)
L384@P7: p−2, ..., B(1)2
L385@P7: then p is an exponent satisfying Fermat’s last theorem.
L386@P7: There is also a related open problem [10]:
L387@P7: Open Problem 1 (Regular Primes). A prime p is called regular if it does not divide any
L388@P7: of B(1)
L389@P7: p−2, . . . , B(1)2 . Prove that there are an infinite number of regular primes.
L390@P7: The following lemma will be useful in proving our last theorem.
L391@P7: Lemma 6 (Applications).
L392@P7: (i) B(−1) x = 2x.
L393@P7: (ii) If x < z, then B(−n) x < B(−n) z .
L394@P7: (iii) If x < z and y < z and n > 1, then B(−n) x + B(−n)
L395@P7: y < B(−n) z .
L396@P7: Proof. Clearly all column vectors are Lonesum (since a column vector is the column of its
L397@P7: row sums), and the number of binary x-tuples is 2x, which proves (i).
L398@P7: To prove (ii), we can embed the Lonesum x×n matrices in the z×n matrices by padding
L399@P7: with zero rows or one rows at the bottom. This gives disjoint embeddings.
L400@P7: To prove (iii), embed the x × n Lonesum matrices in the z × n Lonesum matrices by
L401@P7: padding with zero rows at the bottom, and embed the y × n Lonesum matrices in the z × n
L402@P7: Lonesum matrices by padding with one rows at the bottom. These embeddings are disjoint,
L403@P7: and for any n-tuple not all one or zero, the matrix with this row vector repeated z times is
L404@P7: a Lonesum z × n matrix in neither of the x × n or y × n embeddings.
L405@P7: We can deduce the following theorem.
